meaning: The number 603,550 represents the exact count of Israelite men recorded in the census taken in the wilderness, as stated in both Exodus and Numbers.
description: In Numbers 2:32, the total number of men over twenty years old fit for war from all the tribes of Israel—except the tribe of Levi—is given as 603,550. The same figure appears in Exodus 38:26, where it is linked to the half-shekel tax: each man paid a half shekel according to the sanctuary weight as a contribution toward building the tabernacle. In this way, the census served a dual purpose: it mapped out the military strength of the people and secured funds for the sanctuary. The number symbolizes the greatness of God's people Israel and His fulfillment of the promise to Abraham of becoming a numerous nation. At the same time, the census highlights God's care for each individual within the community—every person was counted and taken into account.

versions.meaning: The number 603,550 represents the exact count of Israelite men recorded in the census taken in the wilderness, as described in Numbers (Bemidbar).

In Jewish tradition, this number has also been linked to the idea that there are 600,000 Jewish souls, which connects to the approximately 600,000 letters in the Torah, where each soul has its root in one letter. The census further emphasizes God's care for every individual within the community.

footnotes.text: In Jewish mystical tradition, the number 603,550 has been rounded to 600,000 and linked to the idea that there are 600,000 fundamental Jewish souls. This concept is further connected to the belief that the Torah contains 600,000 letters, with each soul rooted in one letter. In reality, the Torah has approximately 304,805 letters, so the number 600,000 is understood as a mystical and symbolic figure rather than a literal count.

The shekel tax (half a shekel) mentioned in Exodus 38:26 has been confirmed archaeologically through the discovery of stone weights marked with the word "beka" from the Iron Age in Israel, including sites near the Temple Mount in Jerusalem.

The exclusion of the tribe of Levi from the census is explained in Numbers 1:49–50 by the fact that the Levites were assigned to serve at the tabernacle and were thus exempt from military service. According to rabbinic tradition, they were also excluded because they did not participate in the sin of the golden calf.
